utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, our next witness is Bedri Hyseni.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Hyseni.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you now please make the solemn declaration by reading aloud the document which will be placed before you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I will. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. Mr. Hyseni, we already have before us statements which you've given in the past, so we know a great deal already about what you have to tell us. The purpose of coming here is so that counsel for the parties, that is the Prosecution and for the accused, can ask you questions to perhaps add to the information you've given, to clarify things, or to challenge what you've said. The important thing for us is to get as much information as possible. We don't really want to hear again what you've already said. We want to hear the answers to the particular questions that are asked. So we would be extremely grateful if you would concentrate on the question that each person puts to you and try to confine your answer to the particular point that is raised with you in each question. If you do that, then you will be doing everyone, including yourself, a great service. Now, the first person to ask questions of you today will be for the Prosecution, Mr. Hannis. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, this witness's evidence is presented pursuant to Rule 92 bis (B). His 92 bis (B) package is Exhibit P2270, which we would tender into evidence. His evidence relates to killings in and deportations from Urosevac, Ferizaj municipality, and is pertinent to paragraph 72(h), 73, 75(h), and 77 of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Hyseni. As Judge Bonomy just said --

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- the Judges already have your evidence in the form of your written statements, but I briefly want to introduce you to them and to cover a few points, and then I'm sure Defence counsel will have some questions for you. First of all, sir, I want to confirm that you are a Kosovar Albanian, born in 1960 in Ferizaj, Urosevac town, and since then you've lived in the village of Biba in that municipality; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I understand that you are married with three children and that you worked as a carpenter, and that from 1991 to 1999 you worked for The Council for the Defence of Human Rights and Freedom in Urosevac, Ferizaj municipality.

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, sir, I have a couple of questions about your 2001 statement, and I'm going to page 4 of the English, the first two paragraphs; in the B/C/S, I believe it's page 3, the fourth and fifth full paragraphs. At that point, Mr. Hyseni, you talk about how before the NATO bombing started there was a build-up of Serb forces in your municipality, and you describe that this was done mainly with police reservist. Can you tell us how you distinguish police reservist from the other police that were already in place? Did they look different, act different, have different uniforms? How did you distinguish them?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: The reservist paramilitary forces were different in terms of age, their behaviour, whereas the regular forces are younger and they look different, if we are talking about the military forces. But this applies also to the police forces as well. This is the difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in that portion your statement, you mention the military. Are you referring to the VJ when you refer to military forces that started arriving about a month before NATO?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: Yes. I'm talking about the VJ, the Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In the next paragraph you say that: "In cooperation with each other," referring to the MUP and the VJ, "they armed the Serbian civilian population." First of all, can you tell the Judges how you know that? How do you know that they armed the Serb civilians?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: I know this also because -- because of the mass media, but also because of the fact that the Serbian population were all armed. Indeed, they had even uniforms. And during the NATO airstrikes, they all wore uniforms and were armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Are you aware of how the distribution of arms was accomplished? Did you see arms being delivered to individual Serbs or Serbs going to some sort of distribution point, or do you know?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: I didn't see that, but I heard it through the mass media that arms were distributed. That happened even earlier. I didn't see the actual fact, but I saw them armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did the Serbian authorities distribute any arms to Kosovar Albanians for the purposes of fighting NATO?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: No, they didn't distribute arms to the Albanians of Kosovo to fight NATO. Even if they had, we would have refused.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I want to go to the next paragraph in your statement. You mention that about a year before NATO airstrikes began that there was a group called the Black Hand in your municipality, and you say about them that they were "armed and did not choose their victim. They killed whomever they wanted, and they used this manner to start the ethnic cleansing of Kosovo." Can you elaborate a little about that? First of all, can you tell us when you first heard of this group, the Black Hand?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: The Black Hand started to operate not one year before the NATO airstrikes, not one year before but some months before. It started to function at the end of 1998, when we Albanians heard of that formation. This Black Hand group, which functioned in Ferizaj, killed two people from the Staro Selo, or old village, as we call it; the name is Selami Nagoshi, and another young man from Leskovc family. I don't seem to remember his name at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, is that the first time that you heard something about the Black Hand, when those two young men were killed?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: It was known among the people. But with the killing of Leskovc who was found on the street dead, killed and massacred, his family said that he was killed by the Black Hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall who you first heard about the Black Hand -- who you heard about them from first?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: About the Black Hand, you're asking me? Nobody told me. It was common knowledge because people were being killed, Albanians, in a mysterious way, and they were terrified. And during those months, until the NATO airstrikes began, we didn't dare leave the house after 6.00. I remember once I saw a car, Golf car, without licence plates, parked in front of my courtyard. I didn't identify who the people in it were.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what was being said about the Black Hand? Who were they reportedly affiliated with or associated with?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: I'm not clear about your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, was this just a criminal gang or were they associated with some organised unit or body? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: Yes. People knew that these groups were composed of Serb civilians, and they were associated with people who used to work in the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And why, in your statement, do you associate their activities with the ethnic cleansing in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: Because people were scared. They wanted to strike fear among the population for them to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. In the next paragraph of your 2001 statement, you say: "In relation to the KLA, the situation imposed the establishment of the KLA." I think I understand what you're saying there, but could you explain to the Judges what you mean by "the situation imposed the establishment of the KLA"?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: Yes. Due to the systematic violence perpetrated against them which led to the revocation of the political status, especially in the last 10 years, this violence was demonstrated, as I said, with the revocation of freedom, of our elementary freedom. So there was nothing left for the Albanians to do but to defend their thresholds. With the growing of the violence by the Serbian forces, the Albanian youth, the most vital part of the population in Kosovo, had to face up to this violence, which was expressed in all domains of life in Kosovo. Therefore, the KLA was formed because there was no way out for the Albanian people of Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I want to move next to page 5, paragraph 2 of the English, page 4, the fifth full paragraph of the B/C/S. Mr. Hyseni, you talk about how the night the NATO bombings, a couple of APCs fired on Biba village as they drove by. Then, in the next two paragraphs, you say that after three days you moved to Sojevo, where you tell us the VJ moved into the school. How did you know about those two events, the village being fired on by the APCs and the VJ moving into the school? Did you see that yourself, or was that reported to you by someone else?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: I saw it with my own eyes. On the 24th of March, the airstrikes started sometime around 8.00 in the evening, and at about 11.00, from a rather hilly place which is situated far from the main asphalt road that leads to Gjilan, I mean 4 or 500 metres away, two APCs came from the town up to the bridge that connects the road Skopje-Gjilan. One of them stopped there; the other went to Sojevo village. In Sojeve we didn't see it, but it started to shell continuously at all the houses. It shelled also the new neighbourhood in Sojevo. When it came to Bebe village, there was continuous fire and the fire hit also my house. During that night I was not at home. In order for my family to feel safer, I brought them to the centre of the village. After three days I passed from Bebe to Sojeve to visit my uncle, and I saw that the army had stationed itself at Sojeve village school, on the 4th of April, and we saw them when they deployed themselves at the school. The village is a rather semi-hilly village so you can see different places in it. Therefore, as I said, on the 4th of April, a unit of the VJ was stationed at the school in Sojeve. On the 2nd of April - I don't want to forget it - three tanks and two anti-aircraft artillery cannons were stationed near my uncle's house in Sojeve. This unit stayed there until the 6th of April. They burnt a house, and then they left, joining the unit that was stationed at Sojeve school.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let me take you to the 6th of April, and now I'm referring to your 1999 statement because you have more details about that event in your first statement. It's in the English at page 2, the last two paragraphs, and the first one on page 3; in the B/C/S, it's the last paragraph on page 2 and the following. You mentioned that 18 Serb paramilitaries and two police came to Sojevo and killed your uncle and his wife. And that's detailed in your statement. You say that you later heard that the commander of this paramilitary group was Novica Mijovic from the village of Nikodim. How did you find out about that? Who told you that Mijovic was the commander of the group that did this?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: On the 6th of April, at around 8.00, this paramilitary group - I describe it as a paramilitary, but there were also police in it, so it was a combined group and we counted them to be around 18 - they entered the Limanaj village of Sojeve village and they set fire on the entire neighbourhood and killed two persons - Hamit Halimi, who was 30 years old, and Qerim Ajvazi, who was around 58, 60. Probably Qerim was injured first, but because there were no citizens to help him and because they were -- they set fire to the houses, he died. I saw it with my own eyes because we buried the bodies after two days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hyseni, this is a good example of what I was asking you to avoid doing. You were asked a very specific question, which was this: "Who told you that Mijovic was the commander of the group that did this?" Now, could you please answer that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. I thought I'd give you a broad description of it, but I'll answer your question. Mijovic is a Serbian from Nikodim village who worked for the Yugoslav army in Ferizaj. And in the neighbourhood I was staying, where my uncle and his wife were killed, my uncle on my mother's side, the population left, and we divided in two parts; one went to Lugu i Zenes and the other part went to a meadow. Mijovic and others seized that group, divided the men from the women, stripped them of all jewels and money, and told them to go to Ferizaj, because, "If you come back, we will kill you." Mijovic was known by many citizens. He was known by Danush Nebiu, who is my uncle on my mother's side. And he told me that Mijovic was leading the group, because he was the one who did the talking. Danush Nebiu told me as well as others.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When did Danush Nebiu tell you about it?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: I heard of it in Sojeve, too, but Danush told me when we were in Stankovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And how did he know about it? Had he seen it himself, or did someone else tell him about it?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: He saw it himself, he and his brothers and all the people of that neighbourhood. They all knew him. His uncle was killed. So the two people, the man and the wife that I mentioned who were killed, are his uncle and his wife.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, was this crime, the killing of your uncle and his wife, was that ever reported by you to the police or by anyone that you know of? Was it reported?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: Nazmi Nebiu and Haxhere Nebiu's killing and the two killings in Limanaj neighbourhood, we reported those killings to no one.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know if Mijovic or any of the men with him on that day were ever charged or punished for those killings?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: I have no information about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know where Mijovic is now?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, in your statement, you go on to tell us how you and others hid in the woods for a few days when you became aware of an order to go to Urosevac. Who gave that order to the civilians to go to Urosevac, Ferizaj?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: We stayed in the forest for four days, and after those four days we received the order to leave from the Yugoslav army that was stationed at the schoolyard and in some houses. The neighbourhood of the mosque, which is the biggest neighbourhood, were ordered to leave, and two persons from that neighbourhood informed us to leave the village in two hours and go towards Ferizaj and Skopje.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were there any instructions about what you were supposed to do once you got to Ferizaj, Urosevac?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In your statement you tell us that on the 10th of April, I believe, you arrived at the entrance to Urosevac but the police redirected you to go to Gjilan. Did they tell you why you should go there instead?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: When we went to the junction that links the road to Skopje, Prishtine, Ferizaj, Gjilan, a police patrol road -- traffic police, it was, returned the convoy to go to Gjilan, and the entire convoy returned to go to Gjilan. Probably the purpose was clear. They wanted us to run out of fuel, and it would be easier for them to maltreat us on the way. Their purpose was to send us to Gjilan, then to Presheve and then Macedonia. Had we followed that road, I'm sure that none of us would have made it to Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I want to show you a map. This would be the Kosovo atlas, Exhibit P615, and I think the particular page we need will be page 24. And you tell us in your statement that you were low on fuel, so you stopped in a village called Slatina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in a minute, you'll have on your screen a map, which I hope will show the area that we've been talking about, your home village of Biba. Now, if we could enlarge the left centre portion. Yes. One more, perhaps. Okay. Now, I don't know if you can see on that map, Mr. Hyseni, your home village of Biba.

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: As well as --

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Can you also see Sojevo and Slatina?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Slatina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: There's a pen there that the usher will hand you, and with that you can actually touch the screen and draw on the screen. And if you would first draw a circle around Biba and put the number 1 there.

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: Number 1. [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And then if you can located and draw a circle and put the number 2 inside it around the village of Sojevo.

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And then finally if -- I don't know. Is Slatina on this portion of the map?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: I can't see Slatine. The juncture is here. The road -- I see the road, but I don't see the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: Just a second. I can't read it very well. Maybe it's Slatine. It's here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. If you can draw a circle around that and put the number 3.

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: [Marks]?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if we could take a screen shot of that and give it the next IC number as an exhibit. We'd tender that at this time. I think we're in the low 30s, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be number IC 000033.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In your statement, Mr. Hyseni, you tell us you stayed in Slatina for about 12 days. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And then on the 22nd of April you returned to Urosevac for about five days.

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I believe in your statement you say that partly because your father-in-law and brother-in-law were staying there and they had been wounded. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know when and how they had been wounded?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: When I went from Slatina to Ferizaj, I actually went to my in-laws', to her father and brother. On the second night of the bombing of the military barracks, the house of my in-law, Ramadani, got hit, and this is when my father-in-law got injured and my brother-in-law lightly injured. Through the media, I was informed about this event while I was in Sojeve, but my wife didn't know and I didn't tell her, actually, before I arrived myself in Ferizaj. My father-in-law's name is Ramush Ramadani and my brother-in-law's name is Fatmir Ramadani.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, you tell us after you'd been there for five days that a group of people from -- is it Nerodimlje village came and you joined them and went to the bus station. Have I pronounced the name of that village correctly?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: Yes. The village of Nerodimlje, yes, it is correct. After the military and police forces entered Nerodimlje, this village was expelled, and part of the population, using some local roads, entered the neighbourhood of my in-laws. This neighbourhood was actually empty. There were only two families. So they spent the night there. About 30 people from Kashtanjeva neighbourhood of Nerodimlje village stayed in my father-in-law's house, and together with them, the following day, I took with me my father-in-law and left for Stankovac. So this happened on the 28th of April, when we arrived at Stankovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And then in your statement you explained how you got on buses, went to Kacanik and then eventually went to Macedonia. When did you return to Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: I returned to Kosova after spending a year as a refugee in Manchester, UK. So I returned to Kosova on the 19th of June, 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You returned to your village of Biba?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: Yes, I returned to my village Biba and I rebuilt my house which had been burnt. And I still live there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Before you left Kosovo in April of 1999, had there been any NATO bombing in your village, in Biba village?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: No. NATO bombing occurred in Ferizaj at the military barracks on the first and second nights of the airstrikes. You can see the town of Ferizaj very well from our village. We noticed when the military barracks were hit. We saw fire also in a part of the town called Remonti i Vjeter. There were Albanian shops in that neighbourhood, and these shops were torched by Serbians. We thought in the beginning that it was caused by NATO airstrikes, but they didn't. They only hit the military barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you: What was the reason you and your family left Kosovo in April, 1999?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: The reason we left Kosova in April, 1999, was the violence exercised by military, paramilitary, and police forces of Yugoslavia, the so-called former Yugoslavia. There was no place that we could stay any longer, because you could never know what tomorrow would bring. So my village was moved out due to an ultimatum, and a part of my family also came to Stankovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions. Defence counsel will have some questions for you, Mr. Hyseni.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: We will follow this order: General Pavkovic, General Ojdanic, Mr. Sainovic, Mr. Milutinovic, General Lazarevic, and General Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Hyseni. I have very few questions for you this morning, and I hope that you can answer them rather briefly and quickly and we'll get through this as quickly as we can. The first -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I first want to talk to you very briefly about the statements you've given to the Office of the Prosecutor. You gave a statement on the 8th of May, 1999, in Skopje, Macedonia, where you were interviewed by Kari Seppanen. Are you familiar with that statement?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you will confirm, will you not, that that statement was read back to you in your language after it had been prepared? You were given an opportunity to make any connections you wanted to make. When you were satisfied that it was accurate, you signed the statement, and you put your initials on each page of the statement. Correct?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: I gave my statement in Macedonia. I was interviewed by Mr. Kari. I think he is from Finland. I was interviewed in not a favourable time because I didn't know where my family was and where some other citizens were. But I gave this statement and it is correct. And I also stated then that in case I was called to testify there would be some changes. I did sign that statement; that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you signed an acknowledgement at the end of it, saying that it was true to the best of your knowledge and recollection, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: Yes, I did sign it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you're not telling this Trial Chamber today, are you, that you didn't take it seriously and you didn't try to tell the truth, are you?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: No. I did tell the truth, as far as I knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And, of course, at that time, that was in May of 1999, just shortly after these events that you were describing had occurred, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: Yes. My statement was taken on the 8th of May, 1999, if I'm not mistaken. It was in May.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. Then you gave another statement to an interviewer for the OTP named Annette Murtagh on the 27th of August and the 1st of September in 2001 in your home village. Again, I just ask you to confirm that that statement was read back to you in your language, that you were given an opportunity to make any changes that you felt necessary, and when you were satisfied that it was accurate, you signed it and put your initials on each page. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct. I signed it. I was interviewed by Annette Murtagh, and I did not amend it by making corrections. I just amended it with specific things. I just wanted to clarify things for the statement to be clearer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And on that you also signed an acknowledgement that it was true to the best of your knowledge and recollection, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. The statement was correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In your first statement of 24 March 1999, that you've now told us was correct, you told the interviewer this, and you confirmed that that was correct by signing the document and putting your initials on this page, on page 2, paragraph 6 in the English: "I was at home with my family when NATO started bombing on 24 March 1999. Our house is in the outskirts of the village. Due to safety reasons, I took my family on the other side of the hill, close to the centre of the village." That's what you said in your statement, isn't it? That first statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have hard copies of the Albanian version if it would be helpful to the witness to have.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It would be fine with me for him to have it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which paragraph? Could you please tell me the number?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's a paragraph that begins with the language -- it's probably the sixth paragraph, if they did the same paragraphs in the Albanian.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It is paragraph 6 on his copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's paragraph six, sir: "I was at home with my family when NATO started bombing ..." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: When NATO started the airstrikes I wasn't at home, I was in my uncle's house. And my entire family was sheltering there because my house is very close on the main road going to Gjilan, and all other relatives came in the central part of the village. And this is what I meant by saying I was home, because we live like more members in one house and we treat each other as family. Because at that time I was not in my actual home.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So in that first statement when you said, "I was at home with my family when NATO started becoming," that was not correct?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: It must be a misunderstanding. And I don't know how my statement was translated. But the fact is that when the NATO airstrikes began, I was not with my family in my actual house. I moved my family to the central part of the village for safety reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In paragraph 17 of that same statement -- excuse me just a minute. In paragraph 17 of your second statement, the one of 2001, in this one you change your view a little bit and you say that you moved to the centre of the village because you were sure the NATO strikes would start, and that everybody who lived close to the main road started to move back to the centre of the village. That's paragraph 16 and 17 of your second statement. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Ackerman, that's what he just said was the situation when he explained the position in relation to the earlier statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, you then said that three days later you decided to move to Sojevo, and I think it was in your first statement you said you did that because, as a member of the Human Rights Council, you were afraid the Serbs might catch you. What do you mean "the Serbs might catch you"? That's paragraph 7 of your first statement.

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: Sir, after three days I moved to Sojeve because it's a mountainous village and it's a little bit further. It is true that I was an activist of the Human Rights Council, and all the members of this organisation were imprisoned at that time. The Serbian regime imprisoned both activists of the LDK and of the Human Rights Council. And what I've stated in the statement is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So you were afraid the Serbs might catch you and put you in gaol because of your work on that council? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: At that time they wouldn't just imprison you, they would just take your life. That's why I left.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, what members of that council were killed at that time? Give us their names, will you, whose lives were taken at that time.

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: Almost all members of that council were in prison at that time. On the 28th of June, 1998, almost all members of the council were imprisoned. And in February, 1999, a collective sentence of 289 months of imprisonment was determined. And I haven't heard of any such violence exercised against activists of different organisations before. I have brought as evidence photographs of a person, how he was maltreated and released seven months after he had served his sentence as innocent. I will explain to this Court, how the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hyseni, I'll just stop you, please. You were asked a specific question again and you're not answering the question you were asked. You said that the Serbs, if they caught you, would just kill you, and you're being asked how many members of the Human Rights Council were killed by Serbs, and to give their names. Now, could you deal with that question, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Members of the Council for Human Rights and Freedoms that were killed, you mean during the bombing or before the airstrikes began?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I mean during this time that you were leaving your village because you were afraid of being caught by the Serbs. You said that during that time they wouldn't just put you in prison, they would kill you. Now, how many of your colleagues on that council during that time were caught and killed? Just tell us who they are, where they were killed. Give us the basis for that conclusion.

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: Because members of the council, who was a member of this council in Prishtina, Bajram Kelmendi and his two sons, were executed by security forces in Prishtina, and therefore every other member was scared.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So you know of one person and his two sons. When did that happen?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: It happened during the first or second night of the airstrikes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, you said in that first statement that we just referred to a moment ago that you left your village because of this fear that you would be caught by the Serbs. Then when you gave your second statement in August and September of 2001, you said you decided to leave Biba because it was overcrowded.

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: It was an option, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you went to Sojevo. Why was Sojevo a safe place? You said you went there for safety reasons. Why was it safe?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: It was safer for me because the houses of my uncles were deeper in the village, not close to the main road used by the military and police forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, there came a time when you went to Urosevac, and you stayed there for, I think, six days and then you decided to leave the country. And what you said in your statement was you decided to leave the country because your brother-in-law was wounded and needed treatment. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we have a reference to where that's the reason for leaving the country?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, you can, Mr. Hannis. You can look at the first statement, paragraph 17, and that just reads: "We stayed there for six days but then decided to leave the country. My in-laws were the only people living in that street. Every night we could hear gunshots being fired. We were scared, but especially the children were scared. My brother-in-law was wounded, and we wanted him to get treatment."

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, is the fact that your brother-in-law was wounded and unable to get treatment there that caused you to leave the country to get treatment for him. Wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: One of the reasons was for him to get treatment, yes. But another reason was that the population in Nerodimlje was expelled and there was nothing else that we could do anymore. We had to join them and go together to Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, nobody came to that house and told you you had to leave, did they?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: Nobody came there, but the continuous gunfire throughout the day and throughout the night, there was no way you could stay there. People had left. Nobody was there. There were houses that had been burnt. Only my in-laws were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You had been hearing gunfire for days and days and days and days, hadn't you?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: Usually during the nights.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And all of a sudden, when it became necessary for medical treatment for your brother-in-law, then fear caused you to leave. Is that the testimony you want to give here?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In your second statement, paragraph 22, you talked about April 10th, 1999. You said you saw tanks and trenches in your father's yard and also in your yard. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I do. On 10th of April, after the ultimatum issued by the regular army stationed at Sojeve school, and after the news was conveyed to us by two members of the mosque neighbourhood, we were expelled from Sojeve. There are two cooperatives there, an agricultural one and one for bees. There were military forces in the yards of my relative, all sorts of military equipment and vehicles, tanks, anti-aircraft vehicles, and I have seen them with my own eyes. There were over 100 of them in the yard of the Biba agricultural cooperative. And I can tell you that these houses were completely burnt. Only my family had 14 of its houses burnt. The damage was estimated to be above 2.5 million euros.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. Your country was being attacked by NATO at the time, and it was very clear to you that the Serb forces were setting up defences by digging trenches and so forth in this village, wasn't it? They were trying to defend your country from the NATO forces, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: No. The NATO forces didn't attack Kosova and the population there. For us, NATO represented freedom-loving forces. And it wasn't necessary to dig trenches in our courtyards. It wasn't necessary to deploy a regular army into the Albanian houses, because the army had its barracks, it had its place where it could be stationed, and not stationing itself in our own houses and set them on fire and violate our properties. And just to prove this to you and to their Honours, I brought with me a document signed by one of your superiors, and here you can see names of some soldiers who were there. I don't know if the Prosecutor's office has that list.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You also said in the next paragraph, on page 23, that there was constant firing from anti-aircraft. This was also during the NATO bombing. You said you didn't know what they were firing at, but isn't it pretty clear that they were firing at NATO aircraft that were bombing the area? That's what you do with anti-aircraft weapons, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: They fired, but the NATO planes never hit that territory. So there was no need for them to fire at NATO planes. They just did that to strike fear among the population, because NATO planes never flew, never struck any time at my village during the time I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So is it your testimony here today that NATO never bombed any part of Kosovo, never bombed any village in Kosovo, never bombed any barracks in Kosovo, never took out any tanks or vehicles in Kosovo, never bombed any Serb military forces in Kosovo? They just weren't there; is that your position?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, that misquotes his testimony. He already said NATO bombed the barracks --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I said they didn't strike -- NATO never struck my village. They struck at the places where Yugoslav army forces were deployed in Kosova. They bombed the barracks in Ferizaj and some tanks in Komogllave village from the road that goes from Fshati i Vjeter to Postoni. I answered, sir, telling you that NATO didn't bomb my village and Sojeve.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you just told us that the Serb forces didn't need to build any defensive resources in your village and should have stayed in their barracks. Now you tell us: "We're being bombed by NATO." That wouldn't have been very smart, would it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's argumentative.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think it's not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think the witness should have the opportunity to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you repeat the question, please, sir. I'm not clear about your question, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Just a few moments ago you said the Serb forces had no business setting up defensive positions in your village and digging trenches; they had barracks they could be in. And then just a moment ago you told us that NATO only bombed barracks. That wouldn't have been very smart for these soldiers, the army, to stay in those barracks being bombed by NATO, would it?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: But it wasn't reasonable either for the Serbian forces to enter Albanian homes and set fire to them and kill people.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We were talking about setting up defensive positions and digging trenches. If you're going to defend your country from an attack, that makes sense, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: The NATO airstrikes were committed to defend that territory and to prevent the genocide perpetrated by Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In paragraph 12 of your second statement - Mr. Hannis visited with you a bit about this this morning - you said that the police forces in the military, in cooperation with each other, armed the Serbian civilian population.

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: Can you repeat the question, please, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I haven't asked a question yet. In your statement you said the police forces, in cooperation with the military, armed the Serbian civilian population. Now, you never saw this happening, did you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Don't -- please don't answer that question. We had this clearly answered already, and you may wish to challenge the answer given, but it doesn't help to ask that question because it was clearly stated in his evidence in-chief that he didn't see it happen. All he saw was the results of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So if you're challenging that, let's move to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you ever do any military service?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: Yes, I did, in 1987 in Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: Postoni.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And once you completed your active military service, then you were automatically part of the reserves, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So you were never part of the army reserve, once completing your active military service?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: I was not a member of the reserve forces, because I concluded my service in 1987. Milosevic came to power in 1988; 1989, he revoked Kosova of its autonomy and all the evil started. There was no way I could be a reservist of that formation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You know, do you not, that when people completed their active duty in the Yugoslav army that they then became part of the reserves and actually maintained a uniform which they kept at home in case they were called up. You know that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: I never kept any reserve uniform, and I never was a reservist.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I didn't ask you if you did. You know that reservists kept their uniforms in their homes, don't you?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: I don't know that, because no one from my family was a reservist, and no one had a uniform at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So is it your testimony to this Chamber that there were all of these Serb civilians who had uniforms and were armed, running around the area creating havoc or whatever? In addition to the legal forces in the area, there were these people?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: The NATO forces didn't create us any problems. Don't mix up the question. The Serbian military police and civilian forces, they did create problems for us, but not the NATO forces. I didn't say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That apparently was mistranslated. I didn't say anything about NATO either. What I asked you was: These civilians that you talked about this morning that had uniforms and were armed, what were they doing with their uniforms and their arms?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: You mean the Serbian civilians?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: The Serbian civilians wearing uniforms killed people. For example, on the 6th of April, in Sojeve, four people were killed. Then killings continued even after we left. After we were moved out 11 persons got killed in Sojeve, until the end of the airstrikes. Or in the old village, Staro Selo, which is divided only from a road by my village, nine people got killed there. The paramilitary forces and the army forces were stationed there. Three persons are still missing, sir, in the old village to this day; Emin Zeka and his two sons. Then four persons were found in a septic hole after the NATO airstrikes ended; they were killed, two brothers and their wives. Then two persons were burned in the old village, together, two elderly people together with their homes. These were committed by these formations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, these uniforms that Serbian civilians were wearing as they went around killing people, did they look the same as the regular VJ uniforms?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: The uniforms of the Yugoslav army and the uniforms worn by some civilians were the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. In paragraph 12 of your second statement you talk about paramilitaries, and you say that the heads of these paramilitaries were in Serbia and they were connected with the Serbian government. What evidence do you have to support that statement? On what do you base that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not sure that question accurately reflects what he said in his statement about which militaries, which paramilitaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, what it says in the statement is this: "Heads of paramilitaries were in Serbia, and those paramilitaries were connected with the Serbian government." Just give us the evidence you have to support that sentence in your statement.

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: Look here, I didn't see the paramilitaries in the old village, but people said there was a group of paramilitaries and they said that they were Seselj's group. The paramilitary groups and the military formations had their leaders, and they were linked with the government, because the so-called Yugoslav government, under Milosevic's leadership, with its institutions or bodies, they had a hierarchy. If they called themselves government officials of a state that wanted to place Kosova under its umbrella, how is it possible, then, that paramilitary forces could operate, along with other forces could operate, at will and kill only Albanians? I don't know of a single case that a Serbian was killed by them. This is why I said, because these powers were given to them by the government, by the state bodies. I remember a statement of General Ojdanic one night before the NATO airstrike, saying that: "We will fight with NATO if it starts strikes, even if we are going to inflict unforeseen victims." We knew that those unforeseen victims wouldn't be Serbs, they would be Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Are you aware that a large number of Serbs were killed in the NATO bombing?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to go back to my question -- the answer, I think, to my question about what evidence do you have for that sentence in your statement about the paramilitaries being connected with the Serbian government is that it's an assumption on your part. Is that true? You don't know that, do you?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: This is not an assumption, sir. The military groups belonged to Arkan. He even had a party which was registered with the Serbian government, and he had his own formations in Kosova. If not in my area, he had them in some other places, and that was common knowledge to all the people. That's why I'm saying that everything was done under the auspices of the government, the so-called Yugoslav government.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, have you had any conversations with anybody that was involved inside the Ministry of Defence or Interior who could tell you exactly what was going on in the Ministries of Defence and Interior during this time? Who did you talk to that worked there that knew all these things? Anybody?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: I didn't talk to anyone, sir, but I know that the Ministry of Defence, which is one of the bodies of the government, has these powers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, you said in your statement, it's the last part of paragraph 12 of your second statement: "Everything was coordinated and under the direction of the Ministry of the Defence and the Interior." Now, how could you know that if you didn't know anybody that was inside who was telling you that? You're just guessing, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: I'm not guessing. I'm just repeating it here: Every state which calls itself a state has its institutions, and in this case this was the Ministry of Defence that was responsible for those forces. This is what I'm saying. In no state can there be paramilitary forces that are outside the control of the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. I have one last question for you. This morning, during your testimony a few moments ago, page 10, line 17, you said that the order for you to leave for Urosevac came from the Yugoslav army. Who actually gave that order? Who, in the Yugoslav army, did that order come from?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: Which date are you talking about? On the 10th, the 10th of April?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm talking about when you were ordered to go to Urosevac, Ferizaj.

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: The order was given by the Yugoslav army. That was a unit of that army that was deployed at the Sojeve school, in the neighbourhood near the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Who gave the order? Who told you? Who in the army told you to leave?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: They gave the order to the neighbourhood there. The neighbourhood I was with, my people, about 100 people, we received this news from some people of the other neighbourhood. They said: "You, too, should leave together with us because otherwise they will do short work of anyone they will find here." So it was the order by the army. It had its own captain.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You didn't receive it from the army, you received it from some other Albanian in the neighbour who told you. An army never told you to go to the Urosevac; right?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: The army maybe didn't know that there were other people in the hinterland of the village. Therefore, they told the neighbourhood of Djeni [phoen], of the mosque, to leave the village in 30 minutes, and we left the village thanking those two persons who brought us the news.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You told this Chamber that the army of Yugoslavia ordered you to leave. Now, tell them who in the army of Yugoslavia ordered you to leave? Or tell them that's not true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, he's answered that question. He's told you how the order was relayed to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Who was the person who told you that they had heard this? The neighbour, who was it?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: There were two persons from Sojeve; Ibri Emini, who has a house in that neighbourhood, and one in the other neighbourhood, and he went to visit his farm. When he saw what was happening, he came to tell us. In the meantime, another person came to tell us to leave as soon as we could. When Emin returned with his car, he told us to leave as soon as we could because the army is -- being forced out by the army unit which was an army unit from Nis.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. That's all the questions I have, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do have some questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I have a few questions for you, but it will be law-related questions since we're both lawyers, as you said you got your degree in Pristina, in 1991, your degree from the law school of Pristina University? Is that the state university in Pristina, the one that you graduated from?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: Yes. I finished the Prishtina University.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes. You mean the state university?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: The Prishtina University. I finished my school in the Prishtina University of Kosova in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: That's right. That's the university where Albanians and Serbs and everybody else studied; is that right? Is that the university?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Everybody studied there.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Well, that's what I was asking. You see, sir, there are some things that you know, that I know, but that the Trial Chamber doesn't know. We're from there; right? We know. In your statement, you said that you only know the Albanian language. It is impossible if you don't know some Serbian at least. If you studied at university with Serbs as well, and if you served in the Serb army, you must know a bit of Serbian.

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: I know some Serbian and some English, but my mother tongue is Albanian. I know Serbian, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Of course, yes. Again -- well, yeah. And you said that you had a scholarship from the factory in Urosevac; right? From when until when did you receive this scholarship from the pipes factory?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: Yes. I got a scholarship from the pipes factory to study.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Of course. I agree. I read it. But I'm just going to ask you what is not contained in your statement. So in your statement, it doesn't say from when until when you studied at university. We know when you graduated, and we do not know for how long you received this scholarship from the Urosevac factory.

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: I received the scholarship from 1983 to 1986, if I'm not mistaken, because many years have passed since then.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Right. But you graduated in 1991; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So that means that you did not receive a scholarship for five years; right? Because you were not a good student, I imagine. You were not taking your exams on time.

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: No, I didn't take.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You were 31 when you graduated; right?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: You cannot call me a good student --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, I hope this is leading to something relevant. I hope this is leading to something relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, yes. My very next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Is that perhaps the reason why you were not admitted to work when you said it was their duty for them to admit you? Because you stopped receiving this scholarship in 1986 and --

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: -- in 1991, why would they admit you, five years later? That's the point.

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: Sir, Mr. Lawyer, what you are asking me is not the focus of the topic for me being here. I think that this Tribunal has other issues to deal with. But I will answer you. This is my personal affair, why I took so long to conclude my studies. As whether I was a good or a bad student, that's my personal affair. It is not correct on your part to put that to me. But nevertheless I'm telling you that I was not accepted in that pipe factory or in some other factory because -- you know the problem of the status of Kosova. You know that Kosova had its political status, and that was the problem for -- the starting point for everything; being dismissed from work, poisoning of the students, dismissal of the doctors, of the police officers, Albanian police officers. We had to establish our own state.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Oh, forget about this poisoning of students. Don't tell me you believe that story. Nevermind. Let's move on to 1991. The factory in Urosevac, they were not giving you a scholarship for five years, and they were not giving you a scholarship because you did not graduate on time. They did not have to employ you; right? Am I not right? Press that button, because you turned off your microphone.

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: No, no. I got the scholarship not from the first year but from the third year of my studies. So I got a scholarship only during the third and the fourth year.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You said that in 1996 -- or, rather, 1986 you last received your scholarship. You graduated in 1995. That is five years later. The factory was not duty-bound to give you employment. Yes or no? Just give me an answer. I mean, for five years you did not receive their scholarship. Why would they have to employ you then?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: I got the scholarship for two years of my studies. The contract expired after 1985. Once you are graduated, according to the contract I had, the factory was supposed to take me back to do the work I was given the scholarship for. It was not that the factory didn't accept me. I didn't ask to go back. But it fired other people. You know the situation with the pipe factory. All the workers were sent -- were dismissed with the police. You have seen that on television, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. So definitely you didn't want to have a job in Urosevac. You didn't go and look for a job in Urosevac. Well, there you are. So --

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: Not that I didn't look for a job. I would have looked for a job, but that was a question of discrimination against the right to work by the Milosevic government, and I was obliged to deal with other works. In my statement, I stated I worked as a carpenter. I worked also as a merchant.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Very well. I understand everything you're saying. Can we finally agree on one thing, that you were not looking for a job in Urosevac? Without going into the reasons why you were not looking for a job there. So you were not looking for a job in Urosevac. I can conclude that; right? In the pipes factory; right? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: I didn't, because of the reasons that I mentioned, because of the violence used.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: No need to proceed any further. Thank you. Fine. So then you worked as a carpenter; right? That's what you said. Did you apply anywhere else for a job as a lawyer, except for the Urosevac factory where you did not work? Did you apply for a job anywhere else as a lawyer? Yes or no? Did you apply to work in a court, in a prosecutor's office? I don't know where else. I mean, if you didn't, you didn't. If you did, you did. Nevermind.

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: Listen, sir, I'm not going to look for a job with a government that revoked the autonomy of Kosova through use of force. How could I do that, with a government that I did not elect? This is clear, sir. This is not the focus of the trial. You are a lawyer yourself. You shouldn't waste time here. We should deal with concrete issues. We are talking about genocide and crimes perpetrated against humanity.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Sir, if you give me shorter answers, we will proceed faster. There is no genocide. It's something that you just invented. Then, in 2002, you made another statement.

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: I'm telling the genocide -- we are dealing with genocide.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You returned in Kosovo, then, and then in August, 2001 - and I see that you were unemployed then - in August 2001, you were still unemployed. Was it the Serbs again who made employment impossible for you? Well, that's what it says here, that you weren't working.

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: No. At the time, I returned from England, sir, and it wasn't easy to find jobs. I competed for two places, and I was accepted by one. Even today I work as a professor, but no state can find employment for a whole army of unemployed people. Things take time. And I'm working now, sir. As I said, I am a professor of justice. I work as a professor of law.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... 2007. I asked you about 2001.

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: I couldn't work in 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: Because I had to reconstruct my property which you destroyed. Not you personally, but the Serbian government.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I kindly ask you to give shorter answers. All right. When you got your degree in law, among other things you took an exam in constitutional law; right?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: Did you pass your examine in constitutional law at university, at law school? I mean when you were studying.

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: I passed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: For heaven's sake, yes or no? Did you pass your exam in constitutional law? Fine. If so, how can you claim that Kosovo was a federal unit? In what constitutional law did you learn that? I claim to you that Kosovo was an integral part of Serbia as an autonomous province, Kosova-Metohija. That's what the constitution said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Is that right or not right? Nevermind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Don't answer that question. Mr. Fila, the first two pages of the statement -- if a --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's on page 1 -- on page 2, rather, in Serbian. One, two, three, four, five, the fifth paragraph, it says --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please listen to me for a moment. The first two pages of that statement contain material that this Trial Chamber is not going to give any weight to on the issues that arise in this trial. They were not the subject of any discussion that Mr. Hannis led with the witness. This is certainly not a witness who can give any opinion on the constitutional position of the relationship between Kosovo and Yugoslavia. So that question is not one for him to deal with. And if you're intending to embark on further questions in relation to the first two pages of this statement, I think you would be very unwise. All you could do is improve the position for the Prosecution. So we'll have a break now and we'll resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it seems this was a favourable break for me since I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: No questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have one question and one question only, and perhaps all I need is five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Hyseni, in both your statements and today during the examination-in-chief you mentioned a person by the name of Mijovic from Nerodimlje. You said on page 9, lines 6 and 7, that this person worked for the army of Yugoslavia. Do you know what his work was with the army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: Mr. Novica Mijovic, first of all, is not from Nerodimlje village but from Nikodim village, but he lived in Ferizaj. He worked with the army of Yugoslavia at the army hall in Ferizaj. I don't know whether he was a procurement officer, but all I know is that he worked with the army. This is how I know him. He worked for the army, and whoever works for the army is a member of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I beg to disagree. When you say he worked for the army, did you know that he was a civilian? And did you know that there were civilians employed with the armed forces carrying out some specific tasks? Are you familiar with that, being an attorney, a lawyer?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: He worked in the army hall. In other words, he served in the army regardless of the fact that he was civilian. And on the critical day when four civilians were killed, he was with this paramilitary group.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: No, I wasn't asking you about the critical day. This will be my last question: I hope you will agree with me, and I will try to jog your memory, that this Mijovic person was an electrician. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: As I said, he worked in the army hall. He could have been an electrician. Maybe. I don't know that. But this is how much I know about him. And I already told you what I knew. Maybe he was an electrician.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I understood. That is all right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Hyseni. My name is Dan Ivetic and I am an attorney from Chicago representing Mr. Sreten Lukic here today. I am joined by my colleagues Branko Lukic and Ozren Ogrizovic. We have just several questions to ask you today, so I would request your indulgence and attention. Now, my first question: I would like to find out a little bit more about your work as an activist with the CDHRF, and specifically, as part of your work with this organisation, did you document or investigate abuses or violations of the law carried out by members of the so-called UCK/KLA?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: If the KLA committed abusements, we would have known that, but we have no knowledge of such activity carried out by the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So it is your testimony here today that you do not know of a single criminal act undertaken by the UCK/KLA within the entire municipality of Urosevac?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, Mr. Ivetic, the statement I have in front of me says that his work there was between 1991 and 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's been corrected to 1999, Your Honour, in the information I received from the Prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. There was supplemental information to that effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, that's interesting, because how would I be aware of that, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know whether it was sent to you or not. I'm advised it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you see, if you give us a statement and then it's going to be corrected and we don't get the correction, then it won't be part of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You're right, Your Honour, unless I lead it live, and I did not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Allow me to repeat my question, perhaps limiting it in scope and time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Is it your testimony, sir, that in the years 1997, 1998, and 1999, while you were working with the CDHRF, that it did not have knowledge of any crimes committed by the UCK/KLA within the Urosevac municipality?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: We didn't have any knowledge of any crimes committed by the KLA, and I personally don't know of any crime committed by the KLA in Ferizaj municipality. I don't have any reason to hide anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, now, in your 1999 statement to the Prosecutor of this Tribunal, you stated that neither you nor any members of your family were members of the KLA. The question I want to ask you is: Were you or any members of your family supporters or sympathisers of the UCK or so-called KLA?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: It is true that we were not KLA soldiers, but the KLA was the army of the people, an army that was forced to defend its thresholds. Of course people supported the KLA, at least on a spiritual level. That was the only force.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, in fact, in your 2001 statement to the Office of the Prosecutor, I believe you acknowledged that there was support in your village, the village of Biba, for the KLA. What form did this support take?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: What form did this support take? Well, the population had high hopes that they will manage to evade the worst, and thankful -- thanks to the international alliance everything ended.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, the question I asked you, sir, was: What support did your village of Biba undertake for the KLA? Let me, perhaps, ask it a different way. Did you provide food and ammunition to the UCK/KLA, the village of Biba?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: I have no knowledge about this. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What percentage of your home village of Biba supported the UCK/KLA?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: The KLA was supported by everyone. What percentage would you like me to state? Everyone supported it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. That suffices. Now, were you aware of any KLA presence, active presence, in your village or in the nearby villages of the Urosevac municipality at any point in time during 1998 and 1999?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: As to where KLA was present, we knew. Not only me, but all of the citizens. They were present in Jezerce village, in the Nerodimlje area, whereas in the villages of my area and my own village, in Biba, Sojeve and Nerodimlje, there was no KLA presence and nobody knew of such a presence. And that's why the greatest number of victims occurred in these areas, because wherever KLA was present the number of victims was smaller.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You mentioned Jezerce. Is it correct that there was a KLA command post in the village of Jezerce in the municipality of Urosevac?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: Of course. I believe there was, but I don't know. I can only speak about the municipality where I live. The Nerodimlje zone is well known to the international community, not only to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: A few moments ago during questioning from my colleague you seemed to indicate that even civilians working with or for the Yugoslav army were, in your mind, considered to be members of the army. Let me ask you about the civilians working with or for the KLA. Were there civilians within the ranks of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: The question is not clear to me. Can you please repeat it and be more specific?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. You said you had knowledge of where the KLA was in the municipality and that it was supported by your village. Were there civilian fighters within the KLA structure?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: I don't know that there were civilian fighters within the KLA structure. To my knowledge, they must have been all uniformed, because for someone to be called a formation, a KLA, they have to carry the insignia, and their insignia was known. I don't know of any civilian who was a KLA soldier and wore civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I believe in one of your statements you identify four individuals from your village who joined the KLA. Did they walk around in uniform?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: Who are you referring to? Which four persons?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Were there people from your village who, at some time joined the KLA/UCK?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: After the airstrikes, there were three or four persons who found it easier to join, but I was not in the village when they joined. I heard about it in Stankovac. Up to the airstrikes, there was nobody who joined.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to then go through some more events to find out exactly what it is you saw and what it is you heard about from other people. Now, in your statement, you -- first of all, let's focus on the 1999 statement. You described the critical event that occurred on 6 April 1999, when some forces entered Sojevo and killed your aunt and uncle. And in your 1999 statement - at the Albanian page 3, paragraph 4; B/C/S page 3, paragraph 2; English page 2, paragraph 9 - you stated that you were 100 to 120 metres from the front yard of your uncle's -- of your uncle's residence when the shooting occurred. However, in your 2001 statement - at the Albanian page 6, paragraph 5, going on to page 7, paragraph 1; the B/C/S page 5, paragraph 1; the English page 5, paragraph 6 - in that statement you said that as soon as you saw the forces come into the village, you and your family went to the woods with 230 other people. Now, how do you reconcile these two versions? Were you actually in the woods or were you near your uncle's home when these forces entered that home?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: These forces killed two persons in Limanaj neighbourhood and torched the entire neighbourhood. We evacuated one part of the population. When we saw that all the houses in Limanaj neighbourhood were on fire, we came back and evacuated the population. And these very same forces entered the Shulaj neighbourhood, or the neighbourhood of Shukri Begu, how we call it. I was at about 100 or 120 metres from the house where my uncle from my mother's side was Nazmi and his wife Haxhere. So I saw when two paramilitaries entered his courtyard. Haxhere Nebiu was outside the house near the gate, and one of the paramilitaries fired and I heard a terrifying cry produced by Haxhere. So I left in the direction of some bushes and walked towards the direction where entire population was. Later on we came back and found Nazmi and Haxhere. Both of them were killed. We counted 24 cartridges. And this is what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. So I take it that you saw part of the occurrence but not the actual killings themselves. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: If I had seen -- if I hadn't seen --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Correction:

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: If I had seen the killing, I wouldn't have been able to be here and testify. I would have been killed as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
