utterances.text: Okay. Now, you describe in your statement and in your direct testimony that these 18 paramilitaries were accompanied by two persons that you label as policemen. Now, with respect to these two persons that you label as policemen, did you see them clearly, or could you see them clearly from your vantage point?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: We counted about 18 persons who, having torched 90 per cent of that neighbourhood, they killed these two persons, and they used a local road to leave this neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, I asked a very specific question, and the question was: With respect to the two persons you label as policemen, could you see them clearly from your vantage point?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: When the killing occurred, you mean? That's what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You identified them as policemen, and I'm trying to find out whether you could clearly see these individuals and their uniforms from your vantage point at any point in time during this event.

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: From the place where I was hiding when the killing occurred, as I mentioned, two paramilitaries wearing military uniforms, camouflage, and red berets, this is what I saw. And after the neighbourhood was torched, they used this local road, and this is where we noticed them. We saw them. We were very close.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: So there were some policemen as well, and they acted together.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, I've been asking you about the persons that you described as policemen in your statement and during your direct testimony and that you've now just mentioned. I'm asking you: Did you actually see the persons you label as policemen clearly from the vantage point where you were located?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: I did see them, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, the other questions I have for you are relative specifically to these two people that you say were policemen, and I would ask you just to limit your answers to them and we'll get through this a lot quicker and easier. With respect to these two individuals, could you see any badges on their uniform; and, if so, where?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: No. It is very difficult to distinguish badges or insignia when you're not at an approximate distance, but you could tell that it was a police uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you right now about any metallic badges. Did you see any metallic badges on the uniforms?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That question's been answered. Mr. Hyseni, how did you know that the uniforms they were wearing were police uniforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can distinguish the colour from a distance. The army wears either a solid green colour uniform or a camouflage one, while the police wears a blue uniform. And you can see this from a distance. As for the insignia, I'm sorry, but I couldn't see them because I was far.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did these individuals have any belts of any specific colour as part of their uniform? Again, I'm focusing just on the two persons you've labelled as policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: They must have had belts, but I don't know what colour they were. As I said, I was at a considerable distance, and you cannot tell colours from a distance.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You mentioned that the uniform was a blue one. Was it a solid colour or was there a pattern to it?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: It was a blue camouflage one.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Did you see these two individuals arrive in a vehicle; and, if so, what type of vehicle was it?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: These individual entered the neighbourhood where I was staying, but it looks like they came in buses at the end of the village of Shijel [phoen], the road to Gjilan. They said they came from that side. They entered the Limanaj neighbourhood first and then came to Shukri Begu neighbourhood. In the latter they entered this neighbourhood on first.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: When you say in this answer, "They said they came from that side," I take it you did not actually see them enter the village but are relying on what other people told you. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: When they got off, it is about 1.5 kilometres, this location, and I didn't see them. But when they were walking through this meadow, we could see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, you described an individual that you identify as this Mijovic person. Did you see Mijovic with the forces that were in your uncle's yard?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: The distance was about 100 metres. Now, as to my uncle's courtyard, I don't know if it was Mijovic or someone else, but he should know because he was part of that group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We've had this question answered by being told that the information was relayed to the witness when he was in Stankovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I believe that was the information about Mijovic's occupation. It wasn't clear to me that in fact this individual was not with the group, particularly in light of the statements that he has given that seem to indicate that Mijovic was with this group. So that's why I was asking for clarification of that, Your Honour. I've got the clarification --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But that's not what your question was. Your question was whether --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Whether he actually saw him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Saw him.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And I thought we'd already been told that he didn't, but you obviously see it differently.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. And I also have documents that perhaps Your Honours have not seen, so that's why I was trying to clear it up in my own mind before going into area of questioning that would bear no fruit.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, if we could move on to another topic. After this incident, sir, you joined a convoy of people headed towards Urosevac, and you described in your statement how Serbian traffic police turned you back. Now, would it be accurate to state that the direction you were turned back towards was the direction of your home villages?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: No. They told us to go in the direction of Gjilan.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: Is it true that from Urosevac your home village is in the direction of Gnjilane?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: Yes, it is true that my village is in the direction of Gjilan.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Correct me if I'm wrong, but in your statement you said that you yourself did not have any communications with these two persons you identify as traffic police. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: I didn't [Realtime transcript read in error "did"] have communication with them because I wasn't in the first vehicle. The first vehicle was told to go in the direction of Gjilan, with the intention to take the road to Presheve and Bujanovc.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So you don't actually have knowledge of the intentions of the traffic police or what they actually said the convoy should undertake. Am I correct in that?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: I didn't know and have any knowledge at that time, but when we back we learned, because we communicated between each other. They blocked the road and they wouldn't allow us to proceed in that direction. They told us to go in the direction of Gjilan.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, for purposes of the transcript, page 50, line 23, the answer is recorded as saying "I did have communication with them." I heard the translation as saying "I did not ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, Presheve and Bujanovc, those are towns within the Republic of Serbia; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now --

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: They are part of Presheve valley.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, these traffic police that you mentioned, could you describe their uniforms, what their uniforms looked like?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: They had ordinary traffic police uniforms, those that you could see on an everyday basis. One of them had these white sort of sleeves that are usually worn by traffic police.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you note any badges, insignia, or ribbons on these uniforms?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I didn't. They just gave this order for us to go back and we did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You said you could see this uniform on a daily basis. On regular police did you often -- did you -- strike that. In your daily experiences, isn't it a fact that the police uniforms had badges, insignia, and markings on their uniforms?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: They must have had, but I didn't notice it. I wasn't interested in it. I cannot tell you now that they had badges, insignia, and other markings when I didn't observe it. But what I can tell you is that we could recognise what a traffic police was.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, after this incident at the outskirts of Urosevac, you and the others in the convoy with you went to Slatina. And in your 2001 statement you describe how the police would drive through Slatina but did nothing else. Was this on a daily basis, the entire time that you were in Slatina, or how frequent was it?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: No. The police passed two or three times nearby.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: And during the 12 days I stayed there, I saw them only three times. There was a large number of displaced people there coming from many villages of Gjilan and Viti.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: On those three or so occasions when you saw the police in Slatina, the village where you were located at that time, is it correct to state that no one from these police ever ordered you to leave the village of Slatina?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: I left the village of Slatine after 12 days. Nobody ordered me. But some of the displaced people left the place because we were so many in number that there was no food for us. We ran out of short supplies, so we had to leave. However, at the end of May, my uncles who were there - some remained there - were driven out of the village by the police and sent to Macedonia. Some youths were sent to prison in Viti. This happened when I wasn't there, but I heard it from others.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, I thought I asked you earlier - maybe I should repeat it - I'm only interested in what you have direct knowledge of, what you saw, and I believe, based on this answer, that you were not present when this event occurred, so I will move on and clear up a few other points. Now, after you and your family decided to go to the border, in your statements you describe a man named Fishekovic, who you stated was previously a member of the financial police. Now, I just wanted to clear things up for people. This financial police that you describe, that was not -- that entity was not a part of the Serbian MUP, was it?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: The financial police, prior to the bombing, were civilians. That day when I went to Macedonia, at the entrance to Kacanik there was a police checkpoint and some soldiers who stopped the convoy of buses, along with the bus I was in --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We have all that, sir, in your statement. We have all that in your statement. I just wanted to make clear for people who may not know the structure of the MUP that the financial police was not a part of the Serbian MUP. Could you please confirm that for me? Your answer --

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: I never said that the financial police is part of MUP or is not part of MUP. But this person, whom I knew from before as a financial inspector, that day was dressed in green uniform, carrying a rifle on his shoulder and an insignia with two white eagles.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, unfortunately -- I think it's clear from that that the financial police were not a part of the MUP. Now, I'd just like to touch on a few areas from your testimony today. You mentioned at one point in time that there was, to you, a suspicious vehicle, a Volkswagen Golf with no licence plates. You never, in fact, verified the identity of the persons in that vehicle that was near your home, did you?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And the members of the UCK/KLA, what type of vehicles did they transport personnel in, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: I have no knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you discussed the wounding of your father-in-law and brother-in-law, and as I was taking notes on this, there was some question left in my mind: Were they wounded as a proximate result of NATO bombing in Urosevac?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: No. These people were wounded as a result of the fire shot off -- as a result of a shell thrown by the army forces which destroyed part of the house and injured these two people from the Ferizaj barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you talk about hearing of certain things from the mass media. What type of mass media was available to the civilian population of Urosevac in 1999?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: The television, satellite television, that we could watch. So we watched it on television.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And --

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: There was also a newspaper.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Were there newspapers and televisions available in the Albanian language?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: Yes. It was Bujku newspaper. First it was called Rilindja; then it was changed into Bujku. For your information, there was also information provided by foreign stations. We constantly heard BBC, Voice of America, and Deutsche Welle.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you stated that -- in your testimony you stated that you learned of your father-in-law and brother-in-law being wounded on the television when the barracks were attacked by NATO forces. Is it your testimony that the Serb forces were in the barracks at the time that NATO struck the barracks and that is how a shell came into your father-in-law's house?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: The shell came from the barracks. At that moment NATO was not bombing.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I believe that's different from your testimony, but I will move on to try and finish up your examination. Now, with respect to -- you identified a member of your organisation named Kelmendi. How did you find out about what happened to Mr. Kelmendi? Was it also through some form of mass media?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: We heard of Mr. Kelmendi's killing through the media. First he was kidnapped by the Serb security.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, with respect to hearing things through the media, isn't it a fact that the Albanian language media also reported the killing of Mr. Ibrahim Rugova in 1999, also by Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: This is not true, and I never heard that news.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And, in fact, Mr. Rugova was not killed. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: No, he was not killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you suggesting, Mr. Ivetic, that Kelmendi was not killed?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I do not have knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You don't know about him, do you?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I do know -- I'm just saying the things from the media, the occurrences as reported in the media, may not be 100 per cent accurate, is all that I'm trying to find out, and he answered that he didn't know, so I'm done with that line of questioning. And I think I'm actually done with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. All right. Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was considering whether I would stipulate to the fact that the media doesn't always report things 100 per cent accurately, but I have no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hyseni, in the course of your evidence you mentioned twice that you had brought documents with you; on one occasion you mentioned photographs and on the other occasion you mentioned a document that listed personnel, army personnel, who were present somewhere. So that you leave here with no doubt about the Trial Chamber's position, I should explain to you that the presentation of evidence here is a matter for the -- principally for the parties involved, and it's for the Prosecution to decide whether they present certain things to us. Don't be concerned that because we do not ask you for these documents that something is going wrong. We rely on the Prosecution, having investigated the things that you would bring with you or that you have to tell them, and we leave it to them to decide, generally speaking, what material to present. So we have the full picture now. That completes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give it. You're now free to leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours, and all the others. And I wish you good health and successes in your work for justice to come to light.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hyseni.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. The next witness is Hazbi Loku. We intend, as indicated in the notification, to make an application that his statement be received under Rule 89(F). However, with your leave, there would be a couple of corrections and a couple of exhibits which I think I should go through with him. I'm sure I will be able to do that well within one hour. The relevant paragraphs to which his evidence most directly relates to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You've actually found a witness who has only given one statement, have you?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: One OTP statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: One OTP statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. We can have Mr. Loku, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: While he's coming in, the paragraphs are paragraph 72(k)(i), 75(k)(i) and Schedule K. May I also announce that with us is Mr. Januz Zielinski, one of our legal interns who has been of great assistance in preparing this and other witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Loku.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you now please make the solemn declaration by reading aloud the document which will be placed before you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Loku, good morning.

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I know you have already been told that the Judges have had a copy of your statement, indeed all the parties have had a copy of your statement, and therefore this morning I will be taking you through some areas of the statement. So I want you to testify with that knowledge, that we are already aware of most of what you have had to say on the matters that you're here to testify about. Firstly, could you just identify yourself by giving us your name and spelling your last name?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: Yes. My name is Hazbi Loku, L-o-k-u.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And where do you live, sir?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: I was born in Kotline, Kacanik municipality. For the moment, after the war, I've been living in Ferizaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The village of Kotlina, you told us in your statement, was a wholly -- or was wholly populated by Albanian -- or Kosovo Albanian people. Can you tell us what the entire population of the village was in, say, February/March, 1999?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: Kotline village was inhabited only by Albanian population. Never was there any other ethnicity living there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And about how many people lived there in February or March, 1999?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: The village had approximately 450 to 500 inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, you recall giving a statement to investigators of the OTP, that's the Office of the Prosecution, on the 4th of June, 1999, about events that occurred in your village in that year?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you signed that statement as being correct and true?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You have had an opportunity to have that statement read back to you. And, for the record, do you still agree that the statement is correct and true, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: For the record, may I just indicate that that is P2296.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: At page 2 of that statement, in the third paragraph you describe events that occurred in your village on the 9th of March.

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you said at one part that houses had been knocked down by tanks being driven into them. Can you tell us if that is entirely correct, or, if not, explain how were houses knocked down by the tanks?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: Yes. On the 9th of March, 1999, in my village of Kotline --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would ask my learned friend of the Prosecution to explain exactly which village this is when he's talking about tanks and houses. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I thought we were dealing with Kotlina, but is there some other village in issue here?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Actually, I put the question to him as his village, and when I said "his village," I meant Kotlina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. Carry on, Mr. Stamp, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I beg your part, but in that context, as far as I understood the statement, a different village was referred to, Ivaja in the actual statement, which is 4 kilometres to the north of Kotlina, if we're talking about the 9th of March, 1999, that is. That was my understanding of the witness's statement, that he came to Ivaja on the 11th and 12th of March.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, if you just look at the start of his answer, at line 12 of page 60, you will see that we're dealing with Kotlina. "On the 9th of March, in my village of Kotlina ..." And I think we should let him carry on with that answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. I will -- I think I understand the line that my friend is taking, and the witness is here and the witness can clarify what the situation is. May I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said in your statement that houses at a particular place were destroyed by tanks. How did the tank -- firstly, where were these houses, in which village?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: On the 9th, when I was talking about the 9th of March, it was the Kotline village that was attacked. In fact, a neighbourhood called Dreshec of this village. The village was burned. I'm talking about this neighbourhood. The entire neighbourhood, all the houses were burned, because the houses were at some distance away from each other. All of the houses were looted. And on the same day, on the 9th of March, there were two victims from the village, that is, inhabitants of Kotline village.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. I just want to clarify one thing, though. When you said, and I'll just read it in English, and I think you're referring to the village of Ivaja, as was pointed out, "houses had been knocked down by tanks being driven into them." Can you just explain how the houses were knocked down?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: In the case of Ivaja village, I may tell you that the event happened on the 8th, not on the 9th of March. When I went to this village, because it's nearby my village, I saw that most of the houses were burned and they were still in smoke, and that they were destroyed. In the same village, the mosque was also set fire to, and the minaret was half destroyed. As to how these houses were burnt and destroyed, this I cannot tell you because I didn't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Let's move on, then, to the 24th of March. That day you observed events which occurred in your village and its environs. You said in your statement that you went to a place to the south of your village and that you have marked it on a map which you provided with your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown Exhibit P2296, the last page of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you see at the bottom --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Sorry, the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It comes after the declaration. It's a drawing we're looking for.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The next page, please. I think you need to find the English version of his statement. It's the last page there. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you see that hand-drawn map in front of you?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: Yes. It's the map that I drew myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And do you see your signature and the date on the bottom right-hand corner of the map?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you just start by getting an orientation. Your area, your district of Kacanik, is in a -- sorry, Kotlina in Kacanik, is in a hilly, mountainous area; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And the village is in a valley between elevated areas?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. The houses are built in a semi-circular form. On both sides of the road are the houses, as you can see in this drawing. There are roads that go in or out of the village, and I have marked them. One takes you to Ivaje. One links us with the asphalt road to Kacanik. One goes to Gllobocica, a village in the border with Macedonia. And another goes to Strasha village.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. I think it's very clear, but the semi-circular parallel lines across the middle of the map with the small figures looking like squares and sometimes triangles, that is the main road through the village, and those figures are depictions of the houses around that road; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. The houses and the mosque. I have tried to draw the minaret.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: All right. The minaret of that mosque is --

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: The school -- I have marked the place where three school facilities were. Near them is the ambulance, the clinic, and then there was part of a mountain. You can see it some tens of metres away from that group of houses where the mountain starts in the southern part of the village --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Witness, we're going to take it step by step.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I certainly haven't found this too fast, Mr. Stamp. It's pretty clear. I don't know what you think isn't clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you see at the top of the map a "V" and at the bottom of the map a "J"? Can you tell us what those indicate?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: Yes. These are the sides. "J" stands for south and "V", for north.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. And I'd like you to indicate where you were on the hill adjacent to your village. Is that marked on the map?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: You can see on the map that the houses are in a semi-circle and then there are some arable lands there on the southern part of the village. It's an elevated part. It's an old Roman ruins of a castle.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And where is it? Did you mark it on the map, or did you put any writing to indicate where it is that you were?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Please tell us where it is that you were.

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: It is written Kalaja, which is the fortress, which is the southern part of the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. And you're saying you indicated on the map where there are some schools. Where did you indicate that, and how did you indicate that?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: There are three school buildings that I drew on this map, and I have marked them with letters, with "S-H" standing for the first letter of the word "school" in Albanian.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And that is above the structure on the map that looks like a minaret?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: Yes, there. And together with the clinic I have drawn a total of four features.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. We'll get back to the map, but I just want to you something now about the events of the 24th. You said that the women, children, old persons were gathered together by the Serb VJ and police personnel. Well, firstly, where on the map were the people gathered? Can you indicate that?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: Yes. To the south of the houses in the centre of the village. I can show it with my pencil if you want.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. That would be very good. You can put a circle around the area where the people are gathered.

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: The place where the population was gathered, some left out of fear and most of them were expelled by the Serbian police and army. It is here, this part.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You could mark it with a circle directly on the screen, please, sir.

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: Yes. [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much. This map is not fully to scale, so can I just ask you: This group of people were about how far from your vantage point?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: About 150 metres, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. You said in your statement that the women and children and old people were loaded into a lorry. When you say "loaded into a lorry," what do you mean? Who loaded them into a lorry, and how did they load them into the lorry?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: Actually, after the event that had occurred in the village, two green military trucks belonging to the Serbian army had come to take the population, the women and children. I can draw a map how they made this journey. Up to the exit of the village they went on foot, and there they loaded them on the trucks, but not all of them, because there wasn't enough space. Those that were not loaded, they walked on foot along the asphalt road.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let me get straight to the point. When you say they were loaded on the truck, and you said that also some walked on the asphalt road, did the people go on the truck voluntarily and did they go on the asphalt road voluntarily, or were they compelled by the Serb forces to do that?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: They didn't do this journey on a voluntary basis. They were forced to. They were beaten, maltreated, and threatened throughout the journey, up until they arrived in Kacanik.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: About how many people in total were in this group, both on the truck and on foot, that went to Kacanik?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: In total there were about 400 inhabitants on trucks. We, about 100 men from the village, were hiding. We were not with this group of people. People were loaded on the trucks as if they were pieces of wood, not human beings.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: And the others followed on foot, the trucks, and they were all at gunpoint, threatened. And they were told that, "If you do not walk, we will kill you here on the road."

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, you said they were taken to Kacanik. Do you know if your co-villagers remained in Kacanik or did they go or were taken anyplace else? Did they remain in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: Yes, I know that, too. All these people remained in Kosova for that particular time. Women and children got off the truck and were sent to different houses belonging to Kacanik, people from Kacanik, and others were sent to the police station in Ferizaj where they were maltreated for two or three days, and after that they were released. These were men that were sent to the police station in Ferizaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Generally, did the population remain in Kacanik in Kosovo, or did they leave Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: The population remained in Kacanik for some time, but since the Serb forces were attacking Kacanik - and I made mention here of the Rakovc massacre - after these events they had to set out for Macedonia. They walked for several nights on mountain paths and finally arrived in Bllaca, which is a place in Macedonia where many people from Kosova arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: My family was part of this group that arrived at Bllaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, in your statement you describe that a group of young men, in excess of 20, had sought to flee to the north side of the village and were captured.

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: Yes. The Serb forces, including the army and the police, had encircled the village and we were under threat and danger. Therefore, we decided to leave, and everybody chose the place where they would go to. I, for example, positioned myself at the fortress; some others in other parts of the village; those who had the houses near the mountain above the village, they took to this mountain out of fear, and they sheltered there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you described where the 20 or so young men were taken in respect -- taken to a hole -- or may I just ask you to correct something. In your statement you said, and this is at paragraph 5 of the statement, the last -- I beg your pardon. It's page 5, the last paragraph. In that statement you said that the men -- or you know that in the area where the men were taken there was a large hole. Was it one hole or more than one hole that was there?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: If you allow me to elaborate this. These men who were hiding in this part of the forest --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Remember that I'm interested in this statement. I just wanted to correct something first. Your statement refers to a hole. Was there one hole or more than one hole on the hillside?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: There were two holes close to each other. Maybe there were 5 to 6 metres between the two of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: I have written here "gropa", a hole in Albanian, which also has the meaning for plural.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And when you say you have written "gropa", you mean it is on the map, the map which you drew for us to show us what happened in your village?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: Yes. It is the northern part of the village, and I have written there "Holes," and it's at the entrance to the village, near the entrance.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, about how far was that from where you were, these holes?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: From the place where I was hiding, as the crow flies, it was about 5 to 600 metres far. Not more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. I think this is pretty clear, but may I just go over it again: You were on a hillside to the south, the village was in between, and the hole where the men were taken was on a hillside to the north.

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: But the village was in a valley, so it did not impede your view of what was happening across the valley. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: No, it did not impede my view at all. You could see everything clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you tell us briefly what you saw happen to the captured men in the vicinity of that hole or those holes?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: Yes. These men that were captured, the majority of them were young. They were youths of 16 years of age. They were taken from the place in the mountain where they were captured, and they stopped and were taken to the direction of the clinic. In the afternoon, after 2.00, they set out in the direction of the holes. They didn't know, and we didn't know either, what was going to happen to them. The people who had their hands tied were taken there, and that's where the maltreatment started, the beating. There were cries. And on the basis of these cries that we could hear, they were thrown in these holes. They were massacred. And in the end, in the evening, the --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said there were -- sorry. You said they were thrown into the holes. After they were thrown into the holes, what happened in respect to the holes?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: After they were thrown into the holes, the holes were mined. An explosion was heard and smoke was seen. And after that, the holes were levelled at the location where the holes were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, this is an appropriate time for us to have a break. Is it an appropriate time to interrupt?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It is. It is convenient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. We will adjourn just now and resume at ten minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I think the first thing I should do is ask the Court if the marked copy, where he marked the villages, would be given a number, an IC number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number IC34, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I was about to move on, but before I do, I noticed, Mr. Loku, that you said after that, after you heard the explosion, the holes were levelled. What do you mean when you say "the holes were levelled"?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: The holes were flattened. The ground was flattened.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could I elaborate a little bit further. Did you see anybody flatten the ground, or was the ground flattened as a result of the explosion that you heard?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: This occurred because of the explosion.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I see. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown, Your Honours, Exhibit P00360.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you identify what that picture is showing?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: Yes. This is the photograph of the holes that were in the mountain above the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know approximately when this photograph was taken?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: It was taken in the autumn, after we returned in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. And that is what I'd like to get to now. You said in your statement that you went to Macedonia where you stayed for some time, and then -- and in Macedonia you discovered exactly the identities of the men who were killed in your village on the 24th. Did you gather photographs of those men and submit them to the OTP?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: When I went to Macedonia, for these persons that were later found later in the holes, I didn't know. They were missing persons, and we didn't know whether all of them were in these holes or only some of them. These holes were opened by others, by Austrian forensics who examined the bodies, and in cooperation with family members, they carried out the identification of 22 persons that were thrown in these holes and whom we buried after they were recovered from the holes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When were these holes excavated by the Austrian forensics and the bodies exhumed? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: They were exhumed in autumn, after the inhabitants returned to the village and after KFOR had entered Kosova. Many others came to investigate, and we would direct them to these holes because we knew that our family members were in them. But up until these bodies were exhumed, we didn't know exactly who was in them. And as I said, after they were identified, we buried them and pictures were taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you -- if I may return to another question. Did you take and deliver to us, the OTP, 24 photographs of persons who were killed in your village that day, including those whose bodies were exhumed from those holes?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: The photographs of the massacred persons were brought here by me together with the photographs that were taken during the burial.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, let's go through these photographs one by one.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown Exhibit P380.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This is the first page, I think, on your screen. Is it there yet?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Exhibit 380. Can you identify the persons nine -- the nine persons on that page?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: Yes, I can identify all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you name them, please, from the top row left to right.

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: Yes. Adnan Loku, Ibush Loku, Mina Kuci, Bajram Loku, Zija Loku, Ismet Loku, Sali Vasliu, Naser Loku, and Mahi Loku. Two of them are brothers of Rexhep Loku. One of them was 17 years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we move on to the next page of this exhibit. Can you identify in the same way, from the top row, left to right.

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: Yes. Danush Idriz Kuci, he was attending secondary school, 16 years of age. Serif Kuci. Dzemal Muradem Kuci. And the last one is Vesel Vlashi; he worked in the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you move onto the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: It is the same exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The same exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: From the top to the bottom.

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: May I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, from top to bottom.

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: Yes. The first on top is Nexhad Ferid Kuci; the other one, Sabri Hamed Loku; and the other one is Nasir Fadil Loku. They are relatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, there will be an exhibit led precisely as to which ones were found in the hole, because, as the witness has indicated, there was an Austrian forensic team there. So although there are 24 photos here which, he says, depicts the persons who were killed, there was only some of them - 22, I think - who were found there. But I don't think we need to go into that now as there will be evidence where those -- that subject is clearly identified, unless the Court thinks it's necessary at this stage. And may I just indicate Exhibit 3 -- P381.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is it another exhibit of more photographs?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, is that not only 16?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Thank you, Your Honour. I stopped too early.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we move on to the next page, please. I'm very grateful to the Court. Please go on.

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: May I continue? These two photos are the photos of a son and his brother -- sorry, his father, Sabit and Garep Loku. The son was a student.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And could we move to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: The first two are the brothers Agim and Ismajl Loku. The third is Ismajl Kuci. Below is the 70-year-old man, Zimer Loku. In the middle Milaim Loku. He was my brother. And the last is Neshad Rexha. He was a nephew in the Loku family. On that tragic day he happened to be visiting his uncles in Kotline.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours. I think that is the last page. And I also just wanted to indicate there is an Exhibit P381 which really is a list of the names on Schedule K. I won't direct the Court to that because he has called those names just now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You spoke about some photographs. Could you have a quick look at P48. Sorry, P49. I'm so sorry. Thank you. Could it be enlarged so slightly. While that is being done, Mr. Loku, can you tell us whether or not you took this photograph? And what does it depict?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: Yes, I took the photograph, and it depicts the people who are carrying the coffins of the dead persons exhumated, who were reburied that day. You can see the house of Baki Kuci which has been reduced to ruins. You can see the coffins where the dead persons, massacred persons, are who were reburied. Those in the photo are my co-villagers.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said the house of Mr. Kuci had been reduced to ruins. Do you know how it was reduced to ruins?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: This house was set fire to from inside. You can see that the top is missing, the roof is missing. It used to be a two-storey house.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Who set fire to it; do you know?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: This was torched by the Serbian forces, the military and the police together.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Before I move on to the next photograph, there is -- in your statement - and I refer to page 5, the second paragraph -- the last paragraph on page 5 and the second paragraph on page 6 in the English version, and I think it is the same in the B/C/S version - you said the remaining Serbs started to prepare to burn the houses. You refer to the people involved in the burning of the houses as Serbs. I take it from your evidence just now that when you refer to Serbs, you mean the Serb police and the Serb army started to burn the houses.

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: Yes. I mean the Serbian army and police.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Lukic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would kindly ask my learned friend not to lead the witness in this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I will proceed without leading. I had thought it was a matter of clarification, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we have a look quickly at Exhibit P3 -- I beg your pardon, Exhibit P50, P5-0. Did you take this photograph, and is this -- or does it depict --

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: I don't see any photos here on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you take it, this photograph, and --

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: Yes, I did. It's the same house. You see the coffins, only taken from another angle.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we have a look at Exhibit P48.

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: Would you allow me to add something?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: In this photo that we have here --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: Now I don't have it anymore on my screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What is it you wanted to say about that photograph that you just had?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: I wanted to say that you can see many other ruined and burned houses, because in the first photo you could see only the house of Baki Kuci. In the second you can see the ruins of many other houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, before you have another photograph, could this be expanded a little bit, and could you tell us what is that photograph and what does it depict?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: Yes. I took this photo. This shows the school picture where I used to work. You can see from it that it has been reduced to ruins. We tried to clean up the rubble after we returned from Macedonia, and built a new school on the foundations of the burnt one. And across it you can see the burnt house of Garep Loku.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. In respect to the events of the 24th of March, did you see any person or any group resisting or -- when I say "resisting," firing weapons at the Serbs forces that day?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: Not on this day. There wasn't any holes and anyone firing at the Serbian forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: There wasn't any? You said there wasn't any something. What is that you said?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: I said that no one fired at the Serbian forces from the population, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, the persons who were killed that day, some of whom -- most of whom were excavated -- exhumed, I'm sorry, in autumn, do you know where they were buried?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: Down. Most of them were buried in the schoolyard.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And where were the others --

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: To this day they are still there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And where were the others buried?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said most of them were buried in the schoolyard. Where were the others buried? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: The others were buried in another place, in the cemetery.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What was that other place? Can you just describe it for me, please.

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Some of them were buried at Kacanik cemetery. Those who are not buried at the schoolyard are buried at Kacanik cemetery.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the Kacanik cemetery, was it associated or did it belong to any organisation?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: This I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you hear anything about any organisation that the Kacanik cemetery might have been associated with?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know whether or not any of these persons who are buried in a cemetery that is associated with the KLA?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that my colleague went one step further in terms of leading this witness. The witness gave two answers to the same question, and now he is getting a leading question this third time from my learned friend Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's a different type of leading question from the one you would normally object to, Mr. Visnjic. This is a leading question against his own interests, I suspect. I know that there's a practice in this Tribunal of following an American, English, and Australian practice, and it may be practiced elsewhere, of having to set certain standards before you can view a witness as hostile. There are areas in between, and indeed in my view all areas -- if I had personal control over this, all areas would be open to the same comment that a witness should be examined in a way that's appropriate to the particular issues that arise. Now, you're standing on this objection, are you? You don't want him to ask this particular leading question?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, I'm standing on it. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, what's your response to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think the response is encapsulated in something Your Honour said. It is an exception to the rules, if we're thinking of the strict rules in respect of leading questions, because it would elicit, if a positive answer was given, an answer which is ostensibly against the interest of the asking party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Let's consider that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We do not consider that allowing this question will in any way be unfair to the accused. Where a problem arises and the Prosecution consider that the -- or have the impression, at least, that a full account is not being given by a witness that they have chosen to lead, then, in general terms, it appears to us not unreasonable for them to ask questions which might be viewed as more appropriate for cross-examination, as long as asking these questions does not create any obvious unfairness to the accused. We don't think that this question falls into the category of being unfair and therefore we will allow it to be asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Loku, the question was: Do you know whether or not any of the persons who were buried in the cemetery in Kacanik were associated with the KLA? And do you know or have you ever heard subsequently that that is the case?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: Yes. Other persons were buried in the heroes' cemetery in Kacanik.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And just for clarity, when you say "other persons," you mean some other persons who were killed in your village that day, "that day" being the 24th of March?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: I mean the persons killed on the 24th and on the 9th of March, on both these dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Of those persons, can you say about how many were buried in the heroes' cemetery in Kacanik? You can approximate.

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: Less than half of them. Seven, eight persons. I can't give you an accurate figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And the --

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: Including the persons killed on the 9th of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I see. And the heroes' cemetery in Kacanik, is that cemetery associated with the KLA?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: There is some -- it is associated. It belongs to the KLA cemetery. But not all the persons killed. The description was made by someone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you that. You said: "But not all the persons killed. The description was made by someone else." Are you saying that all the persons -- well, could you explain your last answer? I'll just read it. You said that the cemetery belonged to the KLA. "But not all the persons killed. The description was made by someone else." What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: When I say this, I mean that after the examination of the corpses exhumed from the holes, most of the dead persons found there were buried in the schoolyard. There were two other cemeteries --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Graves, correction.

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: -- and some of those who were exhumed from the holes were buried in the martyrs' cemetery in Kacanik. And you can find them to this day by names and last names.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. While you were in Macedonia, were you interviewed by persons from the OSCE, that is the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe, the KVM mission?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: I know I was interviewed by the OSCE and by the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And in the course of this interview, did you tell the OSCE about the events you witnessed on the 24th of March, 1999, in Kotlina?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours. I have no further questions in chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stamp. Mr. Loku, are you still the principal teacher in the school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have moved to Ferizaj, and I have been living there for four years now. I work in another school.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The school in Kotlina, you said, was rebuilt. Does it function today as a school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it functions as a school today. It was rebuilt, reconstructed. Students were able to return to school, and also teachers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: May I -- may I, before Mr. O'Sullivan proceeds, just say one thing for the record. There is another exhibit listed on his notice. That is Exhibit P26 -- sorry, Exhibit P358, and that is a map taken from the Kosovo atlas which shows Kotlina, Ivaja, and the neighbouring villages which he has described. They are marked there by name, so I don't think I need to take him to that map. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. General Ojdanic, General Pavkovic, General Lukic, Mr. Sainovic, Mr. Milutinovic, and General Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Loku, good afternoon. My name is Tomislav Visnjic. I represent General Ojdanic, and, together with my colleague Mr. Sepenuk, I have a few questions for you. Mr. Loku, let us begin with the events concerning the presence of the OSCE mission in your village. In your statement, on page 00813732, you said that the OSCE mission left your village on the 23rd of March, 1999, in the afternoon. You also confirmed that during the Milosevic trial, on page 2003. I'm asking you this: Is it your testimony here today that the OSCE mission left your village on the 23rd of March, 1999?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: Yes. The OSCE left on the 23rd of March, 1999. We didn't know that they were not going to come back, because they were present in the village at all times between the 10th and the 23rd. But on the 23rd, they left and never came back.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Loku, as regards the date of the 23rd, we have some problems with that, because since the entire OSCE mission and its personnel left the territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia on the 20th of March, 1999, therefore they couldn't have been in your village on the 21st, the 22nd, and the 23rd of March.

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: They were in the village. May I speak?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: We live in the south of Kosova and may be the last to leave, but they were in our area till the 23rd. Somebody from OSCE can verify if this is true or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. While the OSCE was present in your village, were they there around the clock or did they come to visit the village every day?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: In the beginning they would stay during the day and during the night in the village, while in the last couple of days they would come only in the evenings. Since the village was completely dark, there was no electricity and the population and children were traumatised, they would keep their lights of their vehicles on on both sides of the village so that they would not feel that scared.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Loku, this is in your statement. I wanted to ask you this: Did you know that the OSCE, for every one of their visits to your village, needed to gain permission by the Yugoslav authorities? Were you familiar with that? As your village is in the border area.

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Loku, to go back to the events in your village before the 23rd of March --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Before the 24th of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: -- before that date, did you notice whether any of the people in your village carried any clothes of green or camouflage green colour? Any jackets of that nature?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: No. There weren't persons with that kind of uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Before that same date, the 24th of March, 1999, did you notice whether anyone in your village wore camouflage pants or shirts?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: No, I didn't notice that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Did you see anyone wearing a red beret perhaps?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether anyone in your village had or used a Motorola radio device?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Did anyone in your village have or carry semi-automatic rifles of Chinese make?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: There was no weapon in our village. Even the hunting rifles that some villagers had before were taken by the Serbian police.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I suppose that if I asked you whether anyone in your village carried or used an M-95 rifle or if they had any hand grenades, I presume I would get the same answer from you. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do apologise, but we haven't got translation on B/C/S. Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: How far back, Mr. Cepic?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Line --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Page --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Cepic, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We need your microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I do apologise. One more time: Page 84, line 17, from that line we haven't got translation on B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the answer that's been recorded was that: "There was no weapon in our village. Even the hunting rifles that some villagers had before were taken by the Serbian police." And then the next question, which has yet to be answered -- in fact, back to you, Mr. Visnjic. Your question has not been answered, so you'd better ask it again, please. And I take it you are getting translation now, are you?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Loku, if I asked you whether anyone in your village used or carried an M-95 rifle, called Steyr, or any hand grenades, you would answer the same way you answered the previous question. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: As I said, I didn't see a person with a weapon in the village, and to my knowledge there weren't weapons in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we prepare for the witness 3D74, please, while I'm asking the next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Loku, therefore, you had no knowledge about whether there was a storage with equipment in one of the houses of your village and, inter alia, it contained nine sleeping bags, nine soldier backpacks, strengthened soldier pants of green colour, vests, T-shirts, tents, Motorolas, two hand grenades of Chinese make, eight semi-automatic rifles with ten clips and ammunition, an M-95 Steyr rifle, and 30.000 -- excuse me, 224 pieces of ammunition of 7.62-millimetre calibre with a strengthened charge, as well as 2.347 pieces of ammunition of 7.62-millimetre calibre for rifles, automatic rifles. None of this rings a bell; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: I already said that it's not that it doesn't ring a bell to me, but there wasn't any of the things you mentioned in my village. There were no weapons or equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please show 3D74 to the witness, page 3, please. I would kindly ask the usher, since I have a better copy here, to give the hard copy to the witness. Your Honour, as regards this exhibit and the quality of photographs, I wanted to offer some further explanation. Let me just hand this over to the usher. Could we please place it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Loku, do you recognise whether this is a house from your village? Perhaps we could put page 3 on the ELMO. This is 3D74. It's the third page. Mr. Loku, do you recognise this as any of the houses in your village?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: No. I don't think it is a house from my village.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: You can't recognise, or you're certain that this is not a house from your village?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: I'm certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: You are certain this is not a house from your village?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: Yes, I am. On the basis of the photograph, I don't recognise this house as a house from my village, based on the photograph in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Loku. If you look at the other two pages, I suppose you won't be able to recognise the interior of any of the houses in your village. These are pages 4 and 5 of the same exhibit that is before you now.

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU
utterances.text: You can see from the photograph that there is something in the rooms, but I haven't seen these clothes. And I don't think these are rooms of the houses in my village.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Loku.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, perhaps this is a good time for me to interrupt since I am about to move on to another set of documents pertaining to the same issue. But I may leave that until tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Visnjic. Well, Mr. Loku, we have to adjourn there until tomorrow. There's another case occupying this court in the afternoon. So we have to break off and we have to resume your evidence tomorrow. And tomorrow it will be in the afternoon, at 2.15, so you need to be back here in time to start giving evidence again at 2.15 tomorrow. Meanwhile, it's extremely important that you should not discuss your evidence or any of it with any person; that is either the evidence you've given or the evidence you may yet give here. You can talk about anything else with anyone you meet, but please do not discuss any part of your evidence with anyone at all. We'll see you again tomorrow at 2.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 12th day of September, 2006, at 2.15 p.m. 21 22 23 24
